Golden Retrievers look like sunshine with a tail… but underneath all that fluff is a professional retriever, part-time comedian, and full-time emotional support roommate.

Here are 10 things you may not know about Goldens - with a little Peach Cat commentary, because apparently Biscuit requested supervision.

1. They were developed in Scotland in the 1800s, bred to retrieve game from both land and water. Peach: “So the obsession with carrying random objects is technically a résumé skill.”

2. Their famously gentle “soft mouth” was encouraged so they could retrieve without damaging what they carried. Some can even hold surprisingly delicate objects.

3. Goldens often stay puppy-like for YEARS. The body grows up. The goofy little brain sometimes misses the memo.

4. That gorgeous coat is a water-resistant double coat designed for outdoor work. Translation: rain rolls off… but somehow the fur still ends up on everything you own.

5. Retrieving is deeply wired into them. Socks, shoes, toys, towels—if Biscuit proudly delivers something nobody asked for, he considers the mission successful.

6. They’re regularly used as guide, therapy, assistance, search-and-rescue and detection dogs because they tend to combine intelligence with an eagerness to work with people.

7. Goldens are surprisingly athletic. Behind the sweet face is a dog built for swimming, running and spending approximately nine hours convincing you to throw the ball “one more time.”

8. There are noticeable American, British and Canadian Golden Retriever styles, with differences in build, coat and coloring-even though they’re all the same breed.

9. They’re famous for being social, but that sweetness also means many Goldens REALLY want to be included. Bathroom trip? Congratulations, you now have security.

10. And maybe the most Golden Retriever thing of all: they were bred to bring things back to people… and somehow generations later, they’re still happiest when they’re bringing us something.

A ball. A sock. A stick. A little chaos.

Or, on the days we need it most, comfort.

Peach’s official verdict: Golden Retrievers are basically sunshine that learned how to shed.

Biscuit disagrees.

He says it’s “sparkle.”

Reading a Concall, Following the Supply Chain: A Small Texmaco to  Ramkrishna Forgings Connection

One thing I enjoy about reading concalls is that sometimes a small operational comment in one company leads you to another company and gives you a better picture of the industry.

While going through Texmaco Rail's Q1 FY27 concall, I came across a discussion around wheelsets.

Management said that industry production of wheels had been relatively subdued and that Texmaco remains dependent on the Rail Wheel Factory for part of its requirement. At the same time, management clarified that it currently had enough stock and alternative sourcing avenues for its private and export orders, and therefore did not expect a wheelset constraint in the immediate quarters.

That made me curious about the broader wheel supply chain.

A wagon cannot be completed and delivered without critical components such as wheels/wheelsets. 

So even when a wagon manufacturer has a large order book and manufacturing capacity, availability of critical components can influence how quickly that order book gets converted into physical deliveries.

And this is where I came across the Ramkrishna Forgings–Titagarh Rail Systems wheel project.

The important point here is that I am not suggesting Ramkrishna Forgings is setting up this plant specifically to solve Texmaco's wheelset shortage.
Its current disclosed orders are primarily linked to passenger trains, locomotives and other railway requirements.

The interesting connection is much broader.

India has historically depended significantly on imports for forged railway wheels. 

In 2022–23, the government said around 80,000 forged wheels worth approximately Rs 520 crore were being imported, and at the same time highlighted the need to increase domestic manufacturing capacity as railway wheel demand was expected to rise.

The government subsequently opened the space for private players to build domestic wheel-manufacturing capacity.

Ramkrishna Forgings, together with Titagarh Rail Systems, is now building a forged-wheel facility with planned capacity of around 2.28 lakh wheels per year, with project investment of roughly Rs 2,000 crore.

The project has now moved beyond just an announcement. Ramkrishna Forgings has said that trial production has started, with initial samples submitted to Indian Railways. It has also disclosed an order for around 80,000 wheels from Indian Railways, with additional requirements linked to the JV partner.

So the interesting observation for me isn't:
Ramkrishna Forgings will solve Texmaco's wheelset problem.

I don't think the available data supports that conclusion.

The more interesting observation is: Indian Railways has a large and growing requirement for railway wheels, historically relied partly on imports, has been dependent on a limited domestic supply ecosystem, and is now allowing private players to add significant domestic capacity.

That tells us something about the underlying demand-supply situation in the railway component ecosystem.

And when you put that back into Texmaco, the picture becomes clearer.

Texmaco ended Q1 FY27 with an order book of around Rs 9,923 crore, including more than 6,000 freight cars in the freight-car order book. Yet it delivered only around 1,054 freight cars during Q1.

Management has indicated that it has significant manufacturing capacity, but actual production can be affected by the availability of critical components and other execution constraints.

So there are really two separate questions:

1. Is there demand for railway rolling stock?
The large order books across the ecosystem suggest there is significant demand.

2. Can the supply chain add enough capacity to convert that demand into physical production?

This is where investments in wheels, bogies, components and other railway equipment become interesting.

The Ramkrishna Forgings–Titagarh project is therefore useful to me not because it directly fixes Texmaco's problem, but because it is another data point showing that the railway ecosystem itself needs additional domestic manufacturing capacity for critical components.

And this is also why I find reading across companies more useful than looking at one company in isolation.

A comment in a Texmaco concall about wheel availability led me to Ramkrishna Forgings' wheel project, which then led me back to the broader question of Indian Railways' wheel demand, domestic capacity and the government's push to bring in private manufacturing.

There is still a lot more to verify here, especially around actual wheel demand, capacity utilisation, qualification timelines and how much of the new capacity ultimately gets absorbed.

But the broader point is : 

When an industry has strong rolling-stock demand and critical component capacity is being expanded by new private players, it can indicate that the constraint is shifting from "is there demand?" to "how quickly can the ecosystem build enough capacity to fulfil it?"

That's the connection I found interesting while going through the Texmaco concall. Not a direct company-to-company link, but a useful way of understanding the railway supply chain.

🚨 KOTAK MAHINDRA BANK JUMPS OVER 3%: RBI APPROVES ANUP KUMAR SAHA AS NEW MD & CEO

Kotak Mahindra Bank shares rallied sharply on October 1 after the private-sector lender announced Anup Kumar Saha as its next Managing Director and CEO, providing clarity on one of the bank's biggest near-term uncertainties: leadership succession.

The stock rose more than 3% in morning trade and was trading around ₹431.20 at 10:18 AM.

THE BIG ANNOUNCEMENT 🏦

🔹 New MD & CEO: Anup Kumar Saha
🔹 RBI approval received
🔹 Term: 3 years
🔹 Effective from: January 1, 2027
🔹 Succeeds: Ashok Vaswani
🔹 Vaswani's current term ends: December 31, 2026
🔹 Shareholder approval will also be sought

The appointment provides a defined succession path after Vaswani decided not to seek another term.

WHO IS ANUP KUMAR SAHA? 👤

Saha joined Kotak Mahindra Bank in January 2026 and currently serves as Whole-Time Director and Executive Director.

At Kotak, he oversees:

🔹 Retail Banking
🔹 Government Business
🔹 Data Analytics
🔹 Marketing

But his previous experience is particularly interesting.

Before joining Kotak, Saha spent more than seven years at Bajaj Finance and eventually became its Managing Director & CEO.

He also spent around 14 years at ICICI Bank in senior leadership roles.

Overall, Saha brings more than three decades of professional experience, with deep exposure to consumer finance, retail banking, analytics and digital transformation.

THE BAJAJ FINANCE CONNECTION 📊

Saha joined Bajaj Finance in 2017 as President of Consumer Finance and subsequently served in several senior positions, including:

🔹 Deputy CEO
🔹 Executive Director
🔹 Deputy Managing Director
🔹 Managing Director & CEO

Kotak had highlighted earlier that during his tenure at Bajaj Finance, Saha played a significant role in scaling the consumer-finance franchise, digital transformation and customer-focused growth.

WHY THE MARKET IS WATCHING THIS CLOSELY 👀

Leadership succession had become an important overhang for Kotak Mahindra Bank.

When Vaswani announced in June that he would not seek reappointment, Kotak shares fell more than 2% as investors assessed the uncertainty around his successor.

The RBI's approval of an internal candidate now removes a major part of that uncertainty.

Importantly, Saha isn't joining Kotak from outside on January 1.

He is already part of the bank's senior leadership team and has been overseeing major customer-facing businesses, potentially allowing for a smoother transition.

KEY TAKEAWAY 📌

The significance of this announcement goes beyond today's 3% stock move.

Kotak Mahindra Bank is moving from succession uncertainty to a clearly defined leadership transition.

Saha's background also provides clues about areas that could remain important under his leadership:

Retail banking, customer acquisition, digital transformation, analytics and execution.

However, the appointment itself doesn't change Kotak's fundamentals overnight.

WHAT TO WATCH 👀

The bigger questions will be how Kotak performs under the transition across:

🔹 Deposit growth
🔹 Loan growth
🔹 CASA franchise
🔹 Net interest margins
🔹 Retail banking
🔹 Digital customer acquisition
🔹 Asset quality
🔹 Return on equity
🔹 Execution of the bank's existing strategy

For investors tracking the banking sector, leadership uncertainty at Kotak has now reduced considerably.

The next phase will be about execution.

Anup Kumar Saha जनवरी 2026 में Kotak Mahindra Bank से जुड़े थे और फिलहाल Whole-time Director (Executive Director) के पद पर हैं। वह बैंक के Retail Banking, Government Business, Data Analytics और Marketing से जुड़े कामकाज की जिम्मेदारी संभाल रहे हैं।

Saha के पास 32 साल से ज्यादा का प्रोफेशनल अनुभव है, जिसमें करीब 25 साल का अनुभव बैंकिंग और फाइनेंशियल सर्विसेज सेक्टर में है। Kotak से पहले वह Bajaj Finance में कई वरिष्ठ पदों पर रह चुके हैं। इससे पहले उन्होंने करीब 14 साल ICICI Bank में भी काम किया।

Ashok Vaswani का मौजूदा कार्यकाल 31 दिसंबर 2026 को खत्म होगा। उन्होंने व्यक्तिगत कारणों का हवाला देते हुए दोबारा नियुक्ति नहीं लेने का फैसला किया था।
